At a glance

Best months
  • May for the migration on the Gulf of Mexico coast, the Great Lakes and Delaware Bay
  • June and July for Alaska, the mountains and the Arizona monsoon
  • March is the Platte crane peak and the lek season, and winter is the strongest time in Florida, the southwest and the Salton Sea

Birds that decide the trip

Elegant Trogon in the Arizona canyons

The sky island canyons of southeast Arizona are the only place in the United States where Elegant Trogon breeds. Madera Canyon is the classic site, and the mix of habitats in a few kilometres is what makes the whole region work.

When Late April to September, while the birds are breeding in the sycamore canyons.

Where Madera Canyon, Chiricahua Mountains

Colima Warbler in the Chisos

The Colima Warbler breeds in a few of the taller mountains of Big Bend and in no other part of the United States. Reaching it means the walk up into the Chisos from the basin, which is why far fewer people see it than want to.

When April to June, and the birds have largely stopped singing by July.

Where Big Bend National Park, Chisos Basin

Sandhill and Whooping Cranes on the Platte

Around half a million Sandhill Cranes stage on a short reach of the Platte each spring. They roost on the sandbars and feed on waste grain. A handful of Whooping Cranes pass through with them, which is most of what remains of the wild flock.

When Late February to early April, with mid to late March the peak.

Where Platte River, Rowe Sanctuary

Red Knot on Delaware Bay

Red Knots time their northbound passage to the horseshoe crab spawning on Delaware Bay and feed on the eggs to fuel the rest of the flight. The crab harvest and the knot decline are tied together, which is why the bay is watched so closely.

When Mid to late May, matched to the horseshoe crab spawning.

Where Delaware Bay, Cape May

Black-capped Petrel off Hatteras

The Gulf Stream runs closer to shore off Cape Hatteras than anywhere else on the Atlantic coast, which puts Black-capped Petrel and other deep-water seabirds within a day trip from the beach.

When May to August, when the boats run most often and the specialities are most likely.

Where Cape Hatteras

Iiwi in the Hawaiian rainforest

The Hawaiian honeycreepers came from a single finch ancestor and radiated into dozens of species. What survives now holds on in high rainforest above the elevation where introduced mosquitoes carry avian malaria, which is why altitude matters more here than habitat alone.

When Year round, with drier and more settled weather from April to October.

Where Kokee State Park, Hakalau Forest National Wildlife Refuge

Least Auklet on the Pribilofs

The Pribilof cliffs hold seabird colonies numbering in the millions, and Least Auklet is the most abundant of them. St Paul sits closer to Siberia than to mainland Alaska, so Asian strays turn up alongside the breeding birds.

When Late May and June for the colonies, and September for autumn Asian vagrants.

Where St. Paul Island

Wilson's Phalarope on the Great Salt Lake

The Great Salt Lake is too saline for fish, so its food web runs entirely on brine shrimp and brine flies. That supports Wilson's Phalaropes in hundreds of thousands as they gather before moving south.

When July through September for the phalarope gathering, and April and May for northbound shorebirds.

Where Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge, Antelope Island

When to Go

The United States spans the subtropics to the Arctic, so no single month is best across it. The Gulf coast and the southwest are winter and spring destinations, the north and the mountains have a short summer window, and the two migration peaks move across the country in sequence.

Spring passage

March to May

Migration crosses the country from the Gulf of Mexico coast northward, and the lek season runs before it.

Go for High Island and Magee Marsh take the passerine passage, Delaware Bay fills with Red Knots timed to the horseshoe crabs, and the grouse leks are active from late March.

Trade off Alaska and the northern forest are still closed, and May at the famous sites is crowded.

Typical daily average

The breeding season

June to July

The short northern summer opens everything at once, from the Arizona canyons to the Bering Sea.

Go for Alaska, the Sierra and the northern forest are all reachable, the Maine and Pribilof colonies are full, and the Arizona monsoon brings the hummingbird peak from July.

Trade off This is peak season in the national parks, and the southern deserts are dangerously hot.

Typical daily average

Autumn passage

August to October

Shorebirds move first, then the seabird trips, then the raptor and passerine passage.

Go for Cape May takes its raptor counts on a northwest wind, Point Reyes takes vagrants, the Gulf Stream trips run off Hatteras, and the Bering Sea islands take Asian strays.

Trade off The tundra season closes by early September and the mountain passes follow it.

Southeast Arizona in the monsoon

One canyon at a time through the sky islands, timed for the summer monsoon when the hummingbirds are at their peak. Madera holds the mornings, Ramsey and the Huachucas come next, and the drive east to the Chiricahuas adds the ranges closest to Mexico.

The upper coast first for the Gulf of Mexico crossing and whatever a spring front puts down at High Island, then south to the thorn forest of the lower Rio Grande for the Mexican birds. The hill country on the way back adds the two endangered warblers of central Texas.

The Platte cranes and the prairie potholes

Omaha (OMA), Kearney 3 nights, Valentine 2 nights, Minot 3 nights, back to Minot (MOT)

Half a million Sandhill Cranes on the Platte in March, from a blind booked well in advance, then north through the sandhills to the pothole country of North Dakota. The two halves want different months, so a trip taking both either runs late March into April or splits into two.

Southeast Arizona and the sky islands

Mexican birds at the northern edge of their range, one canyon at a time

The mountain ranges of southeast Arizona stand as forested islands above desert, and each canyon carries Mexican species that reach the United States nowhere else. Madera Canyon is the classic site for finding them, and the mix of habitats in a few kilometres is the reason.

  • Habitat: Sky island ranges rising from Sonoran desert through mesquite grassland and oak woodland into pine and fir at the top. Canyon bottoms hold sycamore and riparian gallery forest, which is where most of the specialities are.
  • When: Late April to September, with the summer monsoon from July bringing the hummingbird peak. Winter is quiet at altitude and the desert below stays productive.
  • Getting there: Tucson is the airport for the whole region. Madera Canyon lies about an hour south, and the Chiricahuas are three hours southeast through Willcox. Ramsey Canyon and Sierra Vista sit in between.
  • Base yourself in: Tucson
  • Look for: Elegant Trogon, Painted Whitestart, Red-faced Warbler, Mexican Jay, Arizona Woodpecker, Rivoli's Hummingbird, Blue-throated Mountaingem, Violet-crowned Hummingbird, Montezuma Quail, Whiskered Screech Owl, Elf Owl, Buff-breasted Flycatcher
  • National parks: Coronado National Forest, Chiricahua National Monument
  • Also covers: Chiricahua Mountains, Chiricahua National Monument, Coronado National Forest, Madera Canyon, Patagonia, Ramsey Canyon, Sierra Vista, Tucson
  • Also watch for: Coati, javelina and black bear in the canyons, with Coues white-tailed deer on the slopes.

The Chihuahuan desert and the Big Bend

A warbler that breeds in one mountain range in the whole country

Big Bend sits inside a loop of the Rio Grande where the Chisos Mountains rise out of the Chihuahuan desert. The Colima Warbler breeds in the taller mountains here and in no other part of the United States, which is why birders make the long drive.

  • Habitat: Chihuahuan desert scrub covers the basin and rises into oak, juniper and pine in the Chisos. The Rio Grande and its wetlands hold riparian woodland that carries Sandhill Crane, waterfowl and other water-dependent birds.
  • When: April to June for the Colima Warbler, which needs the walk up into the Chisos. The desert is at its best in spring, and summer heat on the flats is severe.
  • Getting there: Midland or El Paso are the nearest airports and both are a long drive. The Chisos Basin road climbs into the mountains from Panther Junction, and the Colima Warbler needs the Pinnacles or Boot Canyon trail from there.
  • Base yourself in: Terlingua
  • Look for: Colima Warbler, Lucifer Sheartail, Varied Bunting, Black-capped Vireo, Grey Vireo, Scaled Quail, Zone-tailed Hawk, Common Black Hawk, Mexican Jay, Crissal Thrasher
  • National park: Big Bend National Park
  • Also covers: Big Bend National Park, Chisos Basin, Davis Mountains, Marathon
  • Also watch for: Black bear returned to the Chisos on their own, and the desert holds javelina, kit fox and mountain lion.

The upper Texas coast

The fallout, when a spring norther drops migrants into a coastal wood

Migrants crossing the Gulf of Mexico make landfall on the upper Texas coast, and when a spring cold front meets them over the water they come down into the first trees they reach. High Island is a handful of wooded acres on a salt dome, and in the right conditions it holds numbers no other habitat nearby can.

  • Habitat: Coastal oak and hackberry woodland stands on salt domes above salt marsh, rice prairie and tidal flat. Bolivar Flats is a broad intertidal flat that takes very large shorebird numbers.
  • When: Late March to early May for the migration, with the biggest arrivals on days when a northerly front meets birds over the Gulf. Shorebirds use Bolivar Flats through spring and again in autumn.
  • Getting there: Houston is the airport, about ninety minutes away. High Island sits on Highway 124 near the coast, and Bolivar Flats is reached from the Bolivar Peninsula ferry out of Galveston. Anahuac lies west along the bay shore.
  • Base yourself in: Winnie
  • Look for: Prothonotary Warbler, Cerulean Warbler, Golden-winged Warbler, Scarlet Tanager, Rose-breasted Grosbeak, Painted Bunting, Roseate Spoonbill, Reddish Egret, Piping Plover, American Avocet, Seaside Sparrow, King Rail
  • National park: Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge, Bolivar Flats, Galveston, High Island, Houston
  • Also watch for: American alligator in the marsh, with bottlenose dolphin off the beach.

The Lower Rio Grande Valley

Subtropical thorn forest, and a bird list that belongs to Mexico

The last remnants of subtropical thorn forest along the lower Rio Grande carry a set of birds that reach the United States only here. Santa Ana and Bentsen protect the largest surviving blocks, and the valley towns have built a chain of world birding centres around them.

  • Habitat: Tamaulipan thorn forest and riparian woodland along the river, with resaca oxbows, mesquite scrub and remnant sabal palm. Most of the original forest was cleared for agriculture and what remains is fragmented.
  • When: November to April is the strongest period, when winter visitors add to the residents and the heat has gone. Spring brings raptor passage over the valley.
  • Getting there: McAllen and Harlingen both have airports. Santa Ana lies southeast of Mission on Highway 281, Bentsen is just west of it, and Estero Llano Grande is at Weslaco.
  • Base yourself in: McAllen
  • Look for: Green Jay, Great Kiskadee, Altamira Oriole, Plain Chachalaca, Ringed Kingfisher, Green Kingfisher, Least Grebe, Groove-billed Ani, Olive Sparrow, Long-billed Thrasher, Buff-bellied Hummingbird, Pauraque
  • National parks: Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge, Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Bentsen-Rio Grande Valley State Park, Estero Llano Grande, Harlingen, Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge, McAllen, Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also watch for: Ocelot survives in a few thorn forest blocks, alongside javelina, bobcat and indigo snake.

The Edwards Plateau and the hill country

Two endangered songbirds that breed in central Texas and nowhere else

The limestone hills west of Austin carry the entire breeding range of the Golden-cheeked Warbler, which nests in mature Ashe juniper and oak and in no other habitat on earth. Black-capped Vireo shares the country with it in the scrubbier patches.

  • Habitat: Ashe juniper and live oak woodland on limestone, cut by spring-fed canyons with bigtooth maple at Lost Maples. Scrubby regrowth on the drier slopes is what the vireo needs.
  • When: Late March to early June, when both breeding birds are present and singing. Both have left by July.
  • Getting there: Austin and San Antonio are the airports. Lost Maples is west of Vanderpool on Ranch Road 187, and Balcones Canyonlands lies northwest of Austin near Lago Vista.
  • Base yourself in: Kerrville
  • Look for: Golden-cheeked Warbler, Black-capped Vireo, Canyon Wren, Yellow-throated Vireo, Painted Bunting, Zone-tailed Hawk, Woodhouse's Scrub Jay, Rufous-crowned Sparrow
  • National parks: Lost Maples State Natural Area, Balcones Canyonlands National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Austin, Balcones Canyonlands National Wildlife Refuge, Kerrville, Lost Maples State Natural Area
  • Also watch for: White-tailed deer are everywhere, and the canyon streams hold Guadalupe bass.

The Everglades and the Florida Keys

Caribbean birds at the end of the peninsula, and a tern colony offshore

The Everglades is a shallow river of grass moving south across limestone, and the Anhinga Trail puts wading birds within a few metres of a boardwalk. The Dry Tortugas seventy miles beyond Key West hold the only Sooty Tern and Brown Noddy colony in the United States.

  • Habitat: Sawgrass marsh, cypress dome, mangrove and coastal prairie, with tropical hardwood hammock on the higher ground. The Dry Tortugas are sand and coral keys with almost no cover, which is why migrants there are so visible.
  • When: December to April is the dry season, when wading birds concentrate at the remaining water and the mosquitoes are bearable. Late April is the Dry Tortugas peak for the tern colony and for migrants.
  • Getting there: Miami is the airport and Homestead is the town at the park gate. The Anhinga Trail is four miles inside the main entrance. The Dry Tortugas need a boat or seaplane from Key West, which is a long day from Miami.
  • Base yourself in: Homestead
  • Look for: Snail Kite, Wood Stork, Roseate Spoonbill, Purple Gallinule, Limpkin, Short-tailed Hawk, Mangrove Cuckoo, White-crowned Pigeon, Sooty Tern, Brown Noddy, Masked Booby, Magnificent Frigatebird
  • National parks: Everglades National Park, Dry Tortugas National Park, Big Cypress National Preserve
  • Also covers: Anhinga Trail, Big Cypress National Preserve, Dry Tortugas National Park, Everglades National Park, Homestead, Key West
  • Also watch for: American crocodile and American alligator both occur, along with manatee and the Florida panther.

The Florida peninsula and Merritt Island

Scrub-Jays on white sand, beside a launch pad

Merritt Island shares its boundary with the Kennedy Space Center, and the closed land around the launch pads has protected a large block of coastal marsh and scrub. Florida Scrub-Jay lives in the sand scrub of the peninsula and occurs in no other state.

  • Habitat: Coastal salt marsh, impoundment and mudflat on the lagoon side, with oak scrub on relict dune ridges and pine flatwoods inland. The Ocala sand pine scrub holds the largest remaining scrub-jay population.
  • When: October to April for the wintering waterfowl and waders. The scrub-jays are resident and easiest early in the day.
  • Getting there: Orlando is the nearest large airport and Titusville is the town beside the refuge. Black Point Wildlife Drive runs a loop through the impoundments, and Ocala National Forest lies about ninety minutes west.
  • Base yourself in: Titusville
  • Look for: Florida Scrub Jay, Roseate Spoonbill, Reddish Egret, Wood Stork, Painted Bunting, Red-cockaded Woodpecker, Bachman's Sparrow, Limpkin, Snail Kite, Black Skimmer
  • National parks: Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge, Ocala National Forest
  • Also covers: Lake Kissimmee, Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge, Ocala National Forest, Titusville
  • Also watch for: Manatee gather in the warm-water outfalls in winter, and bobcat and river otter work the impoundment edges.

Cape May and Delaware Bay

A funnel for autumn raptors, and horseshoe crab eggs in May

Cape May sits at the end of a peninsula that concentrates southbound migrants against the Delaware Bay, and the autumn raptor counts there are among the largest in North America. In May the bay shore fills with shorebirds feeding on horseshoe crab eggs.

  • Habitat: Coastal woodland, dune and salt marsh at the point, with broad tidal flats and beaches along the Delaware Bay shore. Bombay Hook on the Delaware side is impounded marsh and mudflat.
  • When: September and October for raptors and passerines, with the biggest days after a northwest wind. Mid to late May for the horseshoe crab spawning and the shorebirds that time their passage to it.
  • Getting there: Philadelphia and Atlantic City are the nearest airports. Cape May Point State Park holds the hawk watch platform, and the Cape May to Lewes ferry crosses to the Delaware shore for Bombay Hook.
  • Base yourself in: Cape May
  • Look for: Red Knot, Ruddy Turnstone, Semipalmated Sandpiper, Sanderling, Peregrine Falcon, Merlin, Sharp-shinned Hawk, Cooper's Hawk, American Kestrel, Northern Harrier, Black Skimmer, Seaside Sparrow
  • National parks: Cape May National Wildlife Refuge, Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge, Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Bombay Hook National Wildlife Refuge, Brigantine, Cape May National Wildlife Refuge, Delaware Bay, Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also watch for: Horseshoe crabs spawn on the bay beaches in May, and bottlenose dolphin work the rips off the point.

The Outer Banks and the Carolina coast

Gulf Stream pelagics, and a woodpecker that needs old pine

The Gulf Stream runs closer to shore off Cape Hatteras than anywhere else on the Atlantic coast, which puts deep-water seabirds within a day trip. Inland the pine savannas hold Red-cockaded Woodpecker, which excavates only in living pines old enough to have heart rot.

  • Habitat: The Outer Banks are a chain of barrier islands, and they carry dune, beach and salt marsh, with maritime forest on the wider islands. Alligator River behind them is pocosin and pine, and the Gulf Stream lies about forty miles offshore.
  • When: May to August for the Gulf Stream trips, when the specialities are most likely. Winter brings large waterfowl and Tundra Swan numbers to the sounds and the refuges.
  • Getting there: Norfolk is the nearest airport. Highway 12 runs the length of the Outer Banks through Pea Island. Pelagic boats leave from Hatteras village, and Alligator River is on the mainland west of the sounds.
  • Base yourself in: Nags Head
  • Look for: Black-capped Petrel, Band-rumped Storm Petrel, Sargasso Shearwater, Cory's Shearwater, Red-billed Tropicbird, Red-cockaded Woodpecker, Tundra Swan, Snow Goose, Piping Plover, Black Skimmer, American Oystercatcher
  • National parks: Pea Island National Wildlife Refuge, Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge, Cape Hatteras National Seashore
  • Also covers: Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge, Cape Hatteras National Seashore, Nags Head, Outer Banks, Pea Island National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also watch for: Red wolves were reintroduced at Alligator River, and black bear are common there.

The Maine coast and the Gulf of Maine

Restored puffin colonies, and an island that fills with migrants

The puffin colonies of the Gulf of Maine were shot out in the nineteenth century and brought back by translocation from Newfoundland, which is why they are now the southernmost in the Atlantic. Monhegan Island ten miles offshore takes migrants in numbers out of all proportion to its size.

  • Habitat: Rocky coast, spruce and fir forest, and low offshore islands with grass and boulder scree where the alcids nest. Acadia adds granite mountain and heath at the coast.
  • When: June and July for the seabird colonies, when the boats to Machias Seal run. Late May and late September for the Monhegan migration.
  • Getting there: Bangor is the nearest airport. Monhegan is reached by ferry from Port Clyde or New Harbor. Machias Seal Island boats leave from Cutler and landings depend on the sea.
  • Base yourself in: Bar Harbor
  • Look for: Atlantic Puffin, Razorbill, Common Murre, Arctic Tern, Roseate Tern, Common Eider, Black Guillemot, Bicknell's Thrush, Blackpoll Warbler, Boreal Chickadee, Spruce Grouse
  • National park: Acadia National Park
  • Also covers: Acadia National Park, Bar Harbor, Machias Seal Island, Monhegan Island
  • Also watch for: Humpback, fin and minke whales feed in the gulf, and harbour and grey seals haul out on the ledges.

The northern forest of New England and New York

Boreal forest reaching south, with a thrush confined to the mountain tops

The spruce and fir of the Adirondacks and the northern Appalachians is boreal forest reaching south down the mountains. Bicknell's Thrush breeds only in the stunted fir near the summits, which gives it one of the smallest ranges of any bird in the region.

  • Habitat: Montane spruce and fir, with northern hardwood forest lower down, and extensive bog and beaver wetland through the Adirondack lowlands. The krummholz near the summits is the thrush habitat.
  • When: June and early July, when the boreal breeders are present and the summit trails are clear. Winter brings finch irruptions in some years.
  • Getting there: Plattsburgh and Burlington are the nearest airports. Saranac Lake and Lake Placid are the usual Adirondack bases, and the bogs at Bloomingdale and Ferd's are the standard boreal stops.
  • Base yourself in: Saranac Lake
  • Look for: Bicknell's Thrush, Spruce Grouse, Black-backed Woodpecker, American Three-toed Woodpecker, Boreal Chickadee, Canada Jay, Rusty Blackbird, Blackpoll Warbler, Mourning Warbler, Evening Grosbeak, Common Loon
  • National parks: Adirondack Park, White Mountain National Forest
  • Also covers: Adirondack Park, Green Mountains, Saranac Lake, White Mountain National Forest, White Mountains
  • Also watch for: Moose have recolonised the Adirondacks, and black bear, beaver and river otter are widespread.

Magee Marsh and the Lake Erie shore

A boardwalk through a wood where warblers wait for a wind

Migrants moving north pile up on the Ohio shore of Lake Erie because they will not cross the open water until conditions suit. Magee Marsh and Ottawa National Wildlife Refuge sit next to each other where Crane Creek reaches the lake, and they hold the largest remaining tract of marshland in the state.

  • Habitat: Marsh, open pools, beach and deciduous woodland on the lake shore. The beach ridge woodland at Magee is narrow, which is what makes the birds in it so easy to see.
  • When: The first three weeks of May, with the second week usually the peak. Autumn passage is longer and much quieter.
  • Getting there: Toledo is the nearest airport, just west along the lake. The sites lie in Ottawa and Lucas Counties off State Route 2, and the Magee boardwalk is signed from the causeway.
  • Base yourself in: Oregon, Ohio
  • Look for: Blackburnian Warbler, Cape May Warbler, Bay-breasted Warbler, Prothonotary Warbler, Connecticut Warbler, Mourning Warbler, Kirtland's Warbler, Scarlet Tanager, Rose-breasted Grosbeak, American Woodcock, Sora, Trumpeter Swan
  • National parks: Ottawa National Wildlife Refuge, Cedar Point National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Cedar Point National Wildlife Refuge, Magee Marsh, Ottawa National Wildlife Refuge, Point Mouillee, Toledo
  • Also watch for: Bald eagles nest in the refuge, and the marsh holds muskrat and mink.

The Platte River and the Nebraska sandhills

Half a million cranes on eighty miles of river, for six weeks

Around half a million Sandhill Cranes stage on a short reach of the Platte in spring. They roost on the sandbars and feed on waste grain in the fields. North of the river the Nebraska sandhills are the largest grass-stabilised dune field in the western hemisphere.

  • Habitat: Braided river with sandbars and wet meadow, backed by cropland. The sandhills behind are mixed-grass prairie on dunes, with interdunal wetlands and lakes.
  • When: Late February to early April for the cranes, with mid to late March the peak. May and June for the grouse leks and the sandhills breeders.
  • Getting there: Omaha is the airport and Kearney is the town in the middle of the crane reach. Rowe Sanctuary runs blinds on the river and they book out well in advance. Highway 2 crosses the sandhills northwest from Grand Island.
  • Base yourself in: Kearney
  • Look for: Sandhill Crane, Whooping Crane, Greater Prairie Chicken, Sharp-tailed Grouse, Upland Sandpiper, Long-billed Curlew, Trumpeter Swan, American Bittern, Bobolink, Grasshopper Sparrow
  • National park: Valentine National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Kearney, Nebraska Sandhills, Platte River, Rowe Sanctuary, Valentine National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also watch for: White-tailed and mule deer, coyote and pronghorn across the sandhills.

The prairie potholes of the northern plains

The duck factory, where the glaciers left the water behind

The retreating ice sheet left the northern plains covered in shallow depressions, and the wetlands in them produce a large share of North America's ducks. The mixed-grass prairie between them carries a set of grassland songbirds that are declining faster than almost any other group on the continent.

  • Habitat: Mixed-grass prairie on glacial till, pitted with shallow seasonal and semi-permanent wetlands. Lostwood and Des Lacs protect large unbroken blocks of it.
  • When: Late May through early July, when the ducks are breeding and the grassland songbirds are singing. The potholes dry through summer in low-water years.
  • Getting there: Minot has an airport and both refuges lie within an hour or two of it. Lostwood is northwest near Kenmare, and Des Lacs runs along the valley north of Kenmare toward the Canadian border.
  • Base yourself in: Minot
  • Look for: Baird's Sparrow, Sprague's Pipit, Chestnut-collared Longspur, LeConte's Sparrow, Nelson's Sparrow, Sharp-tailed Grouse, Marbled Godwit, Wilson's Phalarope, Ferruginous Hawk, Canvasback, Redhead, Ruddy Duck
  • National parks: Lostwood National Wildlife Refuge, Des Lacs National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Des Lacs National Wildlife Refuge, Lostwood National Wildlife Refuge, Medicine Lake, Minot
  • Also watch for: Pronghorn, white-tailed deer and coyote, with Richardson's ground squirrel through the grassland.

Bosque del Apache and the Rio Grande

Cranes and Ross's Geese lifting off flooded fields at dawn

Bosque del Apache is a major wintering site for Sandhill Crane and Ross's Goose, and a stopover for thousands more birds on the Rio Grande flyway. The refuge floods its fields deliberately, and the dawn lift-off from the roost ponds is the reason most people come.

  • Habitat: Managed wetland impoundments and farmed fields on the Rio Grande floodplain, with cottonwood bosque along the river and Chihuahuan desert scrub on the terraces above.
  • When: November to February for the cranes and geese. Sandhill Cranes reach the Rocky Mountain wintering grounds through the autumn and leave through February and March.
  • Getting there: Albuquerque is the airport and Socorro is the town twenty minutes north of the refuge. The tour loop road runs from the visitor centre. Sandia Crest above Albuquerque is the reliable place for the three rosy-finches in winter.
  • Base yourself in: Socorro
  • Look for: Sandhill Crane, Ross's Goose, Snow Goose, Black-crowned Night Heron, Bald Eagle, Brown-capped Rosy Finch, Black Rosy Finch, Grey-crowned Rosy Finch, Scaled Quail, Gambel's Quail, Pyrrhuloxia, Chihuahuan Raven
  • National parks: Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge, Cibola National Forest
  • Also covers: Albuquerque, Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge, Cibola National Forest, Sandia Crest, Socorro
  • Also watch for: Mule deer and coyote work the field edges, and the bosque holds porcupine and beaver.

The Colorado Rockies and the grouse leks

Grouse displaying on the plains at dawn, and rosy-finches on the peaks

Colorado holds displaying grounds for more grouse species than any other state, and the spring lek circuit runs from the eastern plains up onto the sagebrush. Above them the Rocky Mountain passes carry ptarmigan and rosy-finches on the tundra.

  • Habitat: Shortgrass prairie in the east, sagebrush and pinyon-juniper in the west, and spruce, fir and alpine tundra along the divide. The leks are on open ground the birds return to each year.
  • When: Late March through April for the leks, which need a pre-dawn arrival and a booked blind at several sites. July and August for the alpine, once the high passes open.
  • Getting there: Denver is the airport. Wray in the northeast has the Greater Prairie-Chicken leks, Gunnison the Gunnison Sage-Grouse, and Walden the Greater Sage-Grouse. Trail Ridge Road in Rocky Mountain National Park reaches the alpine and closes in winter.
  • Base yourself in: Denver
  • Look for: Gunnison Grouse, Sage Grouse, Greater Prairie Chicken, Sharp-tailed Grouse, Dusky Grouse, White-tailed Ptarmigan, Brown-capped Rosy Finch, Black Rosy Finch, American Three-toed Woodpecker, Mountain Plover, Chestnut-collared Longspur
  • National parks: Rocky Mountain National Park, Arapaho National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Arapaho National Wildlife Refuge, Denver, Gunnison, Rocky Mountain National Park, Walden, Wray
  • Also watch for: Elk, bighorn sheep, moose and pronghorn, with yellow-bellied marmot and pika on the tundra.

Yellowstone and the northern Rockies

Trumpeter Swans that never left, on water kept open by geothermal heat

Yellowstone and the Red Rock Lakes to the west held the Trumpeter Swans that survived when the species was reduced to a few dozen birds. Geothermal water keeps parts of the system open through winter, which is what allowed them to stay.

  • Habitat: Lodgepole pine forest, sagebrush flat, geothermal basin and high wet meadow, with large lakes and the Yellowstone and Snake river systems running through.
  • When: June to September, when the roads are all open and the breeding birds are present. The park roads close through winter except the northern route.
  • Getting there: Jackson and Bozeman are the airports. Grand Teton adjoins Yellowstone to the south, and Red Rock Lakes lies west of the park in the Centennial Valley on unpaved roads.
  • Base yourself in: Jackson
  • Look for: Trumpeter Swan, Harlequin Duck, Barrow's Goldeneye, American Dipper, Clark's Nutcracker, Dusky Grouse, Great Grey Owl, Sandhill Crane, Osprey, Bald Eagle, Mountain Bluebird
  • National parks: Yellowstone National Park, Grand Teton National Park, Red Rock Lakes National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Grand Teton National Park, Jackson, Red Rock Lakes National Wildlife Refuge, Yellowstone National Park
  • Also watch for: Bison, elk, grizzly and black bear, wolf, pronghorn and bighorn sheep.

The Great Salt Lake and the Utah desert

Brine flies and brine shrimp feeding phalaropes in six figures

The Great Salt Lake is too saline for fish, so its whole food web runs on brine shrimp and brine flies, and those support shorebird numbers few wetlands can match. Wilson's Phalaropes gather here in hundreds of thousands before moving south.

  • Habitat: Hypersaline lake with extensive mudflat and playa, fringed by freshwater impoundments where the Bear River comes in. Antelope Island adds dry grassland and sagebrush.
  • When: April and May for northbound shorebirds, and July through September for the phalarope and gull concentrations. Winter brings large numbers of Bald Eagle.
  • Getting there: Salt Lake City airport is close to everything here. Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge is west of Brigham City on a twelve-mile auto tour route, and Antelope Island is reached by causeway from Syracuse.
  • Base yourself in: Salt Lake City
  • Look for: Wilson's Phalarope, Red-necked Phalarope, American Avocet, Black-necked Stilt, Snowy Plover, Long-billed Curlew, California Gull, Black-necked Grebe, White-faced Ibis, Cinnamon Teal, Chukar Partridge, Sage Thrasher
  • National parks: Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge, Antelope Island State Park
  • Also covers: Antelope Island State Park, Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge, Salt Lake City
  • Also watch for: A bison herd runs on Antelope Island, with pronghorn and bighorn sheep alongside it.

Point Reyes and the central California coast

A headland that catches vagrants, and a bay with deep water close in

Point Reyes, on the central California coast, is an outstanding and long-established place for watching migrant waterfowl, shorebirds, raptors and landbirds. Much of it is rolling grassland with clumps of trees that act as magnets for vagrant landbirds, and the Point Reyes Bird Observatory has worked here for decades.

  • Habitat: Sandy beach, mudflat, dune, coastal bays and lagoons, rocky headland, coastal prairie and scrub, salt and freshwater marsh, riparian woodland and coniferous forest across 86,000 acres. Monterey Bay to the south has a submarine canyon that brings deep water close to shore.
  • When: September and October for vagrants at the point, which is what the area is best known for. Monterey Bay pelagic trips run best from August to October.
  • Getting there: San Francisco is the airport and the seashore is on the Marin County coast about twenty miles north. Point Reyes Station is the village at the entrance, and Monterey is about three hours south.
  • Base yourself in: Point Reyes Station
  • Look for: Black-footed Albatross, Pink-footed Shearwater, Ashy Storm Petrel, Rhinoceros Auklet, Tufted Puffin, Marbled Murrelet, Snowy Plover, Wrentit, California Quail, Nuttall's Woodpecker, Allen's Hummingbird, Tricolored Blackbird
  • National parks: Point Reyes National Seashore, Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary
  • Also covers: Bodega Bay, Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, Point Reyes National Seashore, San Francisco
  • Also watch for: Northern elephant seal breed at Chimney Rock, and grey whales pass close inshore on migration.

The Salton Sea and the southern California deserts

An accidental inland sea that is shrinking, and still holds enormous bird numbers

The Salton Sea was created by an irrigation accident in 1905 and has become one of the most important wetlands on the Pacific flyway. It is shrinking and growing saltier, which makes its bird numbers both remarkable and precarious.

  • Habitat: A large hypersaline lake below sea level, with agricultural fields and managed impoundments around its south end. The deserts around it hold creosote flat, palm oasis and Joshua tree woodland.
  • When: November to March, when the wintering waterfowl and shorebirds are in and the heat has gone. Summer temperatures here are among the highest in the country.
  • Getting there: Palm Springs is the nearest airport and Brawley sits at the south end of the sea. Sonny Bono National Wildlife Refuge is on the south shore, Anza-Borrego lies west, and Joshua Tree is north.
  • Base yourself in: Brawley
  • Look for: Yellow-footed Gull, Gull-billed Tern, Wood Stork, White-faced Ibis, Burrowing Owl, Abert's Towhee, Crissal Thrasher, LeConte's Thrasher, Bendire's Thrasher, Gambel's Quail, Verdin, Black-throated Sparrow
  • National parks: Sonny Bono Salton Sea National Wildlife Refuge, Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, Joshua Tree National Park
  • Also covers: Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, Brawley, Joshua Tree National Park, Sonny Bono Salton Sea National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also watch for: Desert bighorn sheep in Anza-Borrego, with kit fox and desert tortoise on the flats.

The Sierra Nevada

Granite, giant sequoia and an alkaline lake full of gulls

The Sierra rises gently from the Central Valley and drops abruptly on its eastern side to Mono Lake, an alkaline lake whose brine shrimp support very large numbers of gulls and phalaropes. The range carries montane forest species through its whole length.

  • Habitat: Mixed conifer and giant sequoia groves on the western slope rise into red fir, lodgepole and alpine granite. The eastern escarpment drops into sagebrush and to the alkaline basin of Mono Lake.
  • When: June to September, once the passes have opened. Tioga Pass through Yosemite usually clears in late May or June and closes with the first heavy snow.
  • Getting there: Reno and Fresno are the nearest airports. Highway 120 crosses Yosemite over Tioga Pass to Lee Vining at Mono Lake, and the pass is closed all winter.
  • Base yourself in: Lee Vining
  • Look for: Great Grey Owl, White-headed Woodpecker, Black-backed Woodpecker, Williamson's Sapsucker, Mountain Quail, Sooty Grouse, Clark's Nutcracker, Pine Grosbeak, Wilson's Phalarope, California Gull, Sage Thrasher, Pinyon Jay
  • National parks: Yosemite National Park, Sequoia National Park, Mono Basin National Forest Scenic Area
  • Also covers: Lee Vining, Mono Basin National Forest Scenic Area, Mono Lake, Sequoia National Park, Yosemite National Park
  • Also watch for: Black bear, mule deer, yellow-bellied marmot and pika, with Sierra bighorn on the eastern crest.

The Klamath Basin and the Cascades

The largest winter Bald Eagle gathering in the lower states

The Klamath Basin refuges sit on the Pacific flyway where Oregon meets California, and the waterfowl passage through them is among the largest on the continent. The eagles follow the ducks, and the winter roost counts here are the biggest outside Alaska.

  • Habitat: Shallow lakes, managed marsh and farmed wetland in a high basin, with sagebrush steppe around and the Cascade volcanoes rising to the west. Malheur to the northeast is a large marsh in high desert.
  • When: March and November for the waterfowl peaks, and December to February for the eagles. Late May and June for the Malheur breeding season and its vagrants.
  • Getting there: Klamath Falls has a small airport and Medford is larger. The refuge auto tour routes run off Highway 161. Malheur is about four hours northeast near Burns, and Crater Lake lies north on Highway 62.
  • Base yourself in: Klamath Falls
  • Look for: Bald Eagle, Ross's Goose, Snow Goose, Tundra Swan, American White Pelican, Sandhill Crane, Bobolink, Franklin's Gull, Black-necked Stilt, Yellow-headed Blackbird, Clark's Grebe, Sage Thrasher
  • National parks: Lower Klamath National Wildlife Refuge, Malheur National Wildlife Refuge, Crater Lake National Park
  • Also covers: Crater Lake National Park, Klamath Basin National Wildlife Refuges, Klamath Falls, Lower Klamath National Wildlife Refuge, Malheur National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also watch for: Pronghorn and mule deer through the sagebrush, with river otter and muskrat in the marsh.

The Olympic Peninsula and Puget Sound

Temperate rainforest, and a murrelet that nests in the canopy

The Olympic Peninsula holds some of the wettest temperate rainforest in North America, and Marbled Murrelet nests high in its old-growth canopy rather than on any cliff or burrow. Puget Sound and the Skagit Flats behind it take large winter waterfowl and raptor numbers.

  • Habitat: Sitka spruce and western hemlock rainforest on the western valleys, with subalpine meadow above and a long wild coast. Inland the Skagit delta is farmland and estuary, and Dungeness is a long sand spit.
  • When: May to July for the forest breeders and the alpine meadows. October to March for the Skagit swans, geese and raptors.
  • Getting there: Seattle is the airport. Port Angeles is the base for the north side of the peninsula and the Hurricane Ridge road. The Hoh rainforest is reached from Highway 101 on the west side, and Skagit is an hour north of Seattle.
  • Base yourself in: Port Angeles
  • Look for: Marbled Murrelet, Rhinoceros Auklet, Harlequin Duck, Barrow's Goldeneye, Trumpeter Swan, Snow Goose, Short-eared Owl, Sooty Grouse, Northern Pygmy Owl, Varied Thrush, Pacific Wren, Chestnut-backed Chickadee
  • National parks: Olympic National Park, Dungeness National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Dungeness National Wildlife Refuge, Olympic National Park, Seattle, Skagit Flats
  • Also watch for: Roosevelt elk in the rainforest valleys, with black bear, river otter and orca in the sound.

Southeast Alaska and the Inside Passage

Glaciers calving into water that seabirds feed in

The Inside Passage is a drowned coastline of steep forested islands and tidewater glaciers, and Glacier Bay takes large numbers of seabirds into water the ice has only recently left. Most travel here is by boat, because roads reach very little of it.

  • Habitat: Sitka spruce and hemlock rainforest to the shoreline, with muskeg on the flatter ground, tidewater glaciers and cold nutrient-rich fjords.
  • When: May to August, when the seabirds are breeding and the boats run. Winter daylight is short and most operators stop.
  • Getting there: Juneau has the airport and is reached only by air or ferry, with no road connection to the rest of the continent. Glacier Bay is entered by boat from Gustavus, and the Alaska Marine Highway links Sitka, Haines and Skagway.
  • Base yourself in: Juneau
  • Look for: Kittlitz's Murrelet, Marbled Murrelet, Pigeon Guillemot, Black Oystercatcher, Harlequin Duck, Barrow's Goldeneye, Bald Eagle, Rufous Hummingbird, Varied Thrush, Chestnut-backed Chickadee, Steller's Jay
  • National parks: Glacier Bay National Park and Preserve, Tongass National Forest
  • Also covers: Glacier Bay National Park and Preserve, Haines, Juneau, Sitka, Tongass National Forest
  • Also watch for: Humpback whale and orca through the passage, with brown and black bear, Sitka black-tailed deer and sea otter.

Denali and interior Alaska

Taiga and tundra on one park road, with a short season to use it

Denali runs a single road ninety miles into the range, and it climbs from taiga through tundra without the walking that most arctic birding needs. The interior around Fairbanks holds boreal species that are hard to reach anywhere else in the country.

  • Habitat: White and black spruce taiga fills the valleys and rises through willow and dwarf birch into open alpine tundra and scree. Bogs and thaw ponds fill the flats around Fairbanks.
  • When: Late May to early July, which is the whole breeding season. The park road opens progressively through May and closes with the first heavy snow.
  • Getting there: Fairbanks and Anchorage both have airports and Denali lies between them on the Parks Highway. Private vehicles are restricted on the park road beyond Savage River, so the shuttle bus is how most people travel it.
  • Base yourself in: Fairbanks
  • Look for: Willow Ptarmigan, Rock Ptarmigan, White-tailed Ptarmigan, Long-tailed Jaeger, Surfbird, Wandering Tattler, American Golden Plover, Northern Wheatear, Arctic Warbler, Bluethroat, Smith's Longspur, Boreal Owl, Northern Hawk-Owl
  • National park: Denali National Park and Preserve
  • Also covers: Anchorage, Denali National Park and Preserve, Fairbanks, Nome
  • Also watch for: Grizzly bear, wolf, caribou, moose and Dall sheep are all regular from the park road.

The Pribilofs and the Bering Sea

Asian strays on American islands, and cliffs holding millions of seabirds

St Paul in the Pribilofs and Gambell on St Lawrence Island sit closer to Russia than to mainland Alaska, and both take Asian birds that reach North America almost nowhere else. The Pribilof cliffs hold seabird colonies numbering in the millions.

  • Habitat: Treeless maritime tundra on volcanic islands, with high basalt sea cliffs, crater lakes and boulder beaches. Gambell adds gravel ridges where migrants shelter in the lee.
  • When: Late May and early June for spring strays and the start of the colonies, and September for autumn Asian vagrants. Weather cancels flights often and trips need slack days built in.
  • Getting there: Both are reached by air from Anchorage, St Paul usually through a charter and Gambell through Nome. Flights are weather-dependent and accommodation on both islands is limited and booked well ahead.
  • Base yourself in: St. Paul
  • Look for: Red-legged Kittiwake, Least Auklet, Crested Auklet, Parakeet Auklet, Horned Puffin, Tufted Puffin, Thick-billed Murre, Red-faced Cormorant, McKay's Bunting, Bluethroat, Arctic Warbler, Common Ringed Plover
  • National park: Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge, Gambell, St. Lawrence Island, St. Paul Island
  • Also watch for: Northern fur seals breed on the Pribilof beaches in very large numbers, and Arctic fox work the cliff bases.

Kauai and the Hawaiian rainforest

Honeycreepers in the last high forest, above the mosquito line

The Hawaiian honeycreepers evolved into dozens of species from a single finch ancestor, and most of what survives now holds on in high rainforest above the elevation where introduced mosquitoes carry avian malaria. Kokee on Kauai and Hakalau on Hawaii are the two most reachable places to see them.

  • Habitat: Ohia and koa montane rainforest on volcanic soil, with the Alakai plateau on Kauai forming a high bog that has kept its forest largely intact. The lowlands are almost entirely converted or invaded.
  • When: Year round for the forest birds, with drier and more settled weather from April to October. The Alakai is one of the wettest places on earth and the trails there flood.
  • Getting there: Lihue on Kauai and Hilo on Hawaii are the airports. Kokee State Park is reached from Waimea on Highway 550. Hakalau needs a four-wheel drive and permission, and access is limited.
  • Base yourself in: Waimea
  • Look for: Iiwi, Apapane, Akiapolaau, Hawaii Amakihi, Kauai Amakihi, Anianiau, Akekee, Akikiki, Nene, Hawaiian Petrel, Newell's Shearwater, White-tailed Tropicbird, Red-tailed Tropicbird
  • National parks: Kokee State Park, Hakalau Forest National Wildlife Refuge
  • Also covers: Alakai Swamp, Hakalau Forest National Wildlife Refuge, Hilo, Kokee State Park
  • Also watch for: Hawaiian monk seal and green turtle use the beaches, and humpback whales winter in the channels.

Preparation

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Sites on this page differ from each other more than any rating could carry, so this is the framework the standard British guides use, and the reserve's own page and warden hold the answers.

  • Permission · some reserves open ground to disabled visitors that is closed to everyone else, and it is granted by asking.
  • Priority · parking bays, hides and the nearest paths are often held for disabled visitors. Ask what is reserved and how to claim it.
  • Parking · how close a car reaches the birds shapes the whole day. Ring ahead for the nearest hard standing to the water or the hide.
  • Paths · surfaces, gradients and gate widths vary inside a single reserve. Ask which trail is boarded, surfaced or level.
  • Perches · a hide with a low window, or a bench where the view opens, turns a viewpoint into a morning.

Every reserve above with its own link carries its access detail there, and a warden answers what a page cannot.
